newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Saudi needs to cut water consumption - experts.
newsitem.headline: Saudi needs to cut water consumption - experts.

text.p: Saudi Arabia faces serious water shortage problems in the future if current levels of consumption are not brought under control, experts said in remarks published on Thursday.
Saudi Arabia depends on scarce rainfall, non-renewable underground water and desalination to supply water for its 18 million-strong population -- which is growing at three to four percent a year.

The government has already taken steps, such as a decision one year ago to stop grain exports, to drastically reduce water use in the desert kingdom. Frequent advertisements on state-run television also call on citizens to stop wasting water.

"It is time that citizens and expatriates in a desert country stop taking this precious commodity for granted and start looking at it more seriously," said Adel Boshnaq, president of technical consulting centre Dar al-Taqniya in the eastern port of Jeddah.
The Arab News daily said Boshnaq was speaking at a conference on the privatisation of the water sector in Gulf states, where water remains heavily subsidised.
Experts at the conference agreed that private companies or independent authorities should gradually take over utility services.

"What is actually happening today is that by continuing water subsidies, Gulf governments are helping the wealthy segments of the society who are the most wasteful in terms of consumption," Boshnaq said.
He said water consumption in the kingdom far exceeded that in countries with renewable, cheap water resources.

The experts estimated urban and industrial consumption of water in Saudi Arabia at three billion cubic metres a year, which could be cut by 25 percent if resources and supply networks were properly used. Consumption could be trimmed by 50 percent if additional investments were made in the sector, they said.

Agriculture consumes 8.36 billion cubic metres of water per year according to estimates by the Ministry of Agriculture and Water Resources and 14 billion cubic metres based on estimates by the Ministry of Planning, the paper said.

After the government's decision to stop grain exports, consumption by wheat farmers dropped to 1,850 million cubic metres in 1996 from 6,990 million cubic metres in 1992, while water used by barley growers fell to 510 million cubic metres from 2,010 million cubic metres in the same period.
